connector: It’s Matthew. Things have been awful quiet at Green Gables, and I don’t rightly know why. Marilla’s got her lips pressed tight, and Anne hasn’t come down. I’m not one to go poking into things. I’ll only say that a house doesn’t feel right when somebody in it is unhappy. Let’s see if we can’t find out what’s wrong.

a.raw: its lovely to be home anne whispered to marilla
a.why: An opening quotation mark and a capital, an apostrophe in the contraction It’s, a comma inside the closing quotation mark, capitals on the names Anne and Marilla, and a period at the end.

b.raw: its time to go home marilla said to anne
b.why: The same pieces: quotation marks around what is said, an apostrophe in It’s because it means it is, a comma inside the closing quotation mark, capitals on both names, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say what Matthew risks by going up, and why he thinks it is worth it.
scholar.journal-q2: … then say whether you think Anne meant her apology, with one detail to back it up.
scholar.journal-q3: … and name a moment when Marilla begins to belong to Anne, too.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Matthew Cuthbert again. I’ll be guiding you today. Here’s the question. By the end of this chapter somebody calls Green Gables home, and you’re to work out what had to happen first for her to feel that way. You’ll look back over the whole week and see how far somebody’s come. And you get to play editor, hunting down apostrophes that went astray.
transcripts.dol: Somebody’s talking again in this model, so look it over slowly. Two of the words have been cut short, and there’s a pause just before the talking stops. Then you find out who said it. The sentence you’re fixing works the same way, and it has a couple of names in it. Look at how the model treats a name before you start on yours. There’s no hurry.
transcripts.guide1: Well now, it’s the last day of the week. You’ve got the same word parts you’ve been working with, and then a choice about what to do with the week’s words. I like that. I’m not much for being told exactly what to do myself. Pick whichever suits you and do it properly. After that there are two drafts to check over, the way a careful editor would.
transcripts.morphology: You’ve matched these before, so this is a check on whether they stuck. Don’t hurry it. If one gives you pause, think of a longer word you know that uses it, and say that word out loud. Most times the meaning’s sitting right there, waiting on you. That’s how I learned my farm tools. By using them, not by reading about them.
transcripts.vocabulary: Four words, and you get to pick what to do with them. If you want my advice, choose the one that makes you think a bit. Explaining a word to somebody younger is harder than it sounds. Whatever you choose, use the word the way the book does, in a real sentence about a real feeling. That’s how a word becomes yours.
transcripts.grammar: Somebody wrote a draft about the chapter. Some of the apostrophes are right and some aren’t. Don’t go tapping every word that has one. Read each sentence as if it were yours and you were about to hand it to Marilla. Would it pass? A sentence might be missing an apostrophe it needs, or have one it doesn’t.
transcripts.spelling: Same sort of job, different draft. Tap only the sentences where an apostrophe is in the wrong place, or missing where it’s wanted. For each one, ask yourself whether the word is just more than one of something, or whether it owns something. That question settles most of them. Take your time over it. There’s no prize for finishing first.
transcripts.guide2: Anne hasn’t come down, and Marilla won’t say why. I’ve been hanging about the kitchen like a lost calf. This week’s watch is belonging, and I’ve been turning it over. I suppose a person can live in a house and not belong to it. As you read, watch the small things. Belonging doesn’t come with a speech. It shows up in some little thing a person does without thinking.
transcripts.wgrd: At the end of a week, it’s worth looking back down the road you came. Think where Anne was when Marilla drove her off to White Sands, and where she’s got to now. Then find one small thing she does today that proves she’s moved. Look at whoever’s standing next to her, too. When one person changes, the folks around them mostly do as well.
transcripts.read: Just one stop today, at the very end, so read straight through till you get there. It’s a short chapter, but there’s a lot in it. When you reach the stop, don’t rush on to the questions. Sit with it a while and think about what one small thing might mean to somebody who’s never had it. I’d wager you’ll know the moment when you come to it.
transcripts.guide3: Well, now you know. I went upstairs. I hadn’t been up there in four years, not since I helped Marilla paper the spare bedroom. I asked Anne if she’d just smooth it over with Rachel, and she said she’d do anything for me. Don’t tell Marilla I had a hand in it. She might think I was putting my oar in. Go on and say what you noticed, and show it from the book.
transcripts.chapter: The first question’s about me, and I’ll admit it’s a bit awkward. Why would a shy old fellow climb those stairs? That’s for you to work out. The second is about Anne saying sorry and Marilla not liking the way she did it, so think about what Anne was doing with her imagination. The last one has you look back over the whole week. Pick your moment, and say why.
transcripts.wordconn: Your vocabulary answer is saved. One of this week’s words was penitent, which is somebody who’s truly sorry. Well, Anne said sorry to Rachel, and Rachel forgave her, and that’s what mattered to me. Whether she was penitent or just enjoying herself a good deal, I’ll leave to you. You’ve read it. I only heard about it.
transcripts.workshop: Your job today is deciding how your character changes from start to finish. Take Anne. When this week began, nobody at Green Gables had asked for her. Now she’s settled, and I think she knows she’s wanted. That’s a long way to come in five chapters. Your character needn’t travel so far. They ought to end the story a little different from how they began, though.
